title: No rule reports a merge commit, so a history meant to stay linear gains them unnoticed
foundBy: user report (host): "Merge commits (errors on new commits, warnings on older that are already pushed)"

evidence.verified: `go test ./internal/oss/ -run 'Merge|Linear' -count=1` passes 3 tests. An unpushed merge in a history of five commits is one error reading `1 of 5 commits are merges`. After a push it is one warning, and in a clone that never fetched it is one warning. A linear history reports nothing. Against the code at 538d036, all three tests fail with `no rule OSS-712`. With the pushed half raised to an error, two of them fail. The binary built at 6b49610 reports 2 of 157 commits as merges in tracer, 3 of 287 in campaign and 1 of 310 in ui, each as a warning. It reports no merge in the other six projects. `make ci` passed at 6b49610.

resolution: OSS-712 reports every merge commit in the history. A merge no remote carries fails the run, because a rebase replays the same work without it. One a remote carries prints as a warning and passes, and so does one in a clone that cannot say what is pushed. A project that merges by design waives the rule with the reason.
details:
The sibling projects keep a linear history. Each change lands as its own commits on `main`, and a branch that fell behind is rebased rather than merged. Nothing checks it. At the time of filing, `git rev-list --merges HEAD` counts 2 merge commits in tracer, 3 in campaign and 1 in ui. Four bring a remote `main` into local work, and two join a finished side branch.

A merge commit is cheap to avoid before it is pushed, because `git rebase` replays the same work without one. Once a remote carries it, removing it rewrites every clone somebody else made. So a merge no remote carries should fail the run. One a remote already carries should be a warning, which is the split the other history rules already make.
